who: Robert McKeaveney (@robertmckeaveney, 653K Instagram followers on 2026-11-27), co-owner of the Wants and Needs clothing brand
read: 2026-11-27, from the on-screen captions of 8 teaching reels (Instagram, signed out) and the transcripts of his YouTube channel @Robertmckeaveney. Paraphrased, not copied.

sources.about: Breakdown of a 2-second reel that got 30,000 followers and sold out a drop
Others copied his format and beat his views: steal formats, add a twist
The hook ladder, with the views each version would get
Tier list: what really matters, what doesn't, what hurts your account
Reading the retention graph: hook, buildup or payoff
Take a viral clip and add a transition into your thing
Every great hook asks a question
10 days of reels before a clothing drop (125K views)

rules.rule: Every great hook makes the viewer ask a question. If they aren't asking one, they have no reason to wait for an answer.
rules.check: stylebrain hooks "LINE" prints its type; a line that fits no type usually asks nothing.

rules.rule: Build the hook in layers. A plain value hook gets stronger with each layer: a bold claim, then the payoff they'll get, then a number, then credibility.
example: This is the best way to add to your bench (+ claim)
The best way to add [x] lb to your bench without more volume (+ payoff)
The [n] changes that added [x] lb to my bench (+ number)
I'm an All-American powerlifter, and these [n] changes added [x] lb to my bench (+ credibility)
rules.check: stylebrain hooks "LINE" prints which layers it has and which to add.

rules.rule: The hook presents the value of the video. Without it there is no reason to keep watching.

Open on proof you can say it: a result you got or a test you ran ("This 2-second reel got me 30,000 followers", "I tested 30 hooks"). For Michael, that's real numbers: All-American, Army powerlifting team, his lifts.
Hook, buildup, payoff. The hook asks the question, the buildup keeps them engaged and strengthens the question, and the payoff answers it so they watch to the end.

Read the retention graph. A drop at the start means the hook failed, a slide through the middle means the buildup failed, and a drop at the end means the payoff failed. A flat line means all three worked.
rules.check: stylebrain retention '[[0,100],[3,70],...]' names the part to fix.

rules.rule: You don't need to reinvent the wheel. Take a format that has already gone viral, add your own topic or a twist, and make it yours. How you structure a topic matters more than the topic itself.
rules.check: stylebrain hooks --examples TYPE --niche NICHE lists proven formats.

rules.rule: For a brand: open on an entertaining viral-format clip (the hook clip), then transition into your thing (for a clothing brand, the edit in the clothes). The entertainment earns the view and the transition carries the brand.

Give people a reason to rewatch. A challenge they can fail by a few frames ("only 1% can pause at the right time") makes them try again, so average watch time can be longer than the video, and Instagram pushes it.
Add one extra layer that converts, like a hidden frame that says "DM us a screenshot for a discount". His version brought in about 29,000 DMs and sold out a drop.

Each video is measured against your baseline. Three weak videos in a row pull the baseline down, and three good ones push it up. Post consistent winners, and hold back a video you expect to flop (he skipped one on drop day).
Post as many quality videos a week as you can make. Posting every day isn't the point.
Use trial reels: A/B test hooks, repost old videos, and get about 5x the output without hurting the main feed.
Calls to action matter, but only after you've given value. Tie the ask to more of the same ("for more content strategies, follow").
Judge each post by views against baseline, watch time and follows per view. His best drop reel got 874K views and 1,300 follows within a day.

doesnt_matter: posting time (a good video wins whenever it goes up)
fancy editing (the edit just has to do its job)
follower count (engagement per video matters more)
hurts: the promote / boost button: he says Instagram then stops recommending your posts organically, so you stay reliant on paying
fits_michael: Use his credibility in the first line: All-American at 516 DOTS, the Army powerlifting team, real PRs (never framed around worlds).
Hook clip plus transition: a funny gym or running bit that turns into a heavy lift, the same way the drop reels turn into the clothes.
Rewatch challenges: "pause when the bar hits depth", "guess the weight before the plates show".
Coaching conversion layer: a frame or a last line that sends people to nospotter.com, only after the value.
Trial reels to test two or three hooks for the same lift before it goes to the main feed.
